title: Proof, Quarantine, and a Clear Path Beyond Vietnam’s Dog Trade
excerpt: Rabies turns delay into death, while stolen-pet claims demand court records. Vietnam needs transparent supply chains, strict quarantine, and abolition by 2030.
body_html:
Rabies gives victims no second chance once symptoms begin. The World Health Organization states that clinical rabies is virtually 100% fatal, yet prompt post-exposure care can prevent death. That public-health reality demands proof, quarantine, and accountability—not slogans defending an opaque trade.

Myths cannot replace records

Claims about stolen family dogs, poison bait, illegal transport, or criminal convictions require named police statements, court judgments, seizure records, dates, and locations. No such incident record appears in current campaign material. Publishing one as fact would mislead families and weaken legitimate reform.

“Farm-raised dogs” also needs evidence: traceable ownership, vaccination records, transport permits, quarantine compliance, inspection history, and humane slaughter safeguards. Without those records, nobody can honestly establish how animals entered a supply chain. That gap does not prove every animal was stolen. It proves public oversight cannot rely on trade assurances.

Biosecurity starts before exposure

Rabies spreads when infected saliva enters bites, scratches, broken skin, or mucous membranes. Handling sick animals, uninspected slaughter, and bite attacks create risk. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. After possible exposure, wash wounds with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and seek urgent medical assessment. Post-exposure prophylaxis includes vaccination and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulin or approved monoclonal antibodies. Care still matters after delay, but treatment must begin before symptoms.

Household exposure incidents and commercial animal transport are parallel biosecurity concerns, not automatically one causal chain. Each demands competent veterinary control, quarantine enforcement, traceability, and public reporting.

Vietnamese communities deserve evidence and protection

Families protecting children, pets, and neighbors need institutions that investigate theft claims, inspect transport, enforce quarantine, and publish decisions. Lawful activity, regulatory breaches, and criminal offenses must remain distinct. Reform gains strength when Vietnamese community leaders, investigators, veterinarians, and families demand records instead of rumor.

State rabies-control targets and SDE’s campaign demand are different. SDE calls for complete abolition of the dog-meat trade by 2030. Add your name to that public demand: sign the national petition, then follow campaign updates on how it reaches decision-makers.
